entry.title: Congress agreed 417–3 on data centers. What else do they agree on?

link.title: Congress agreed 417–3 on data centers. What else do they agree on?

entry.content:
Democrats and Republicans split on most energy votes this term. Then, on September 16, they voted 417 to 3 on one. Here’s what the House actually agrees on, who crosses party lines, and how to look up your own representative before Tuesday.

Energy is one of the most divided subjects in the House. Of the 29 recorded votes on energy bills in this Congress, 83% split along party lines. In September 2025, the GRID Power Act, which tells federal regulators to put “dispatchable” power plants (such as fossil-fuel plants) at the front of the line to connect to the grid, passed 216–206. 2% of Democrats and 99% of Republicans voted yes.

Then came the Ratepayer Protection Act. It asks every state to consider a rule that makes very large data centers (those drawing 100 megawatts or more) pay the full cost of the power lines and upgrades built to serve them, so that cost is recovered from the data center rather than from other customers. It passed 417–3.

That made me want to know what else Congress agrees on. The answer is more than the headlines suggest.

I took every recorded vote in the House since January 2025 (674 of them) and the official topic the Library of Congress assigns to each bill. Here’s what the record shows.

Nearly 4 in 10 votes on bills are bipartisan

Across 420 votes on bills (final passage, fast-tracked bills and amendments), 38% were bipartisan: the share of Democrats and the share of Republicans voting yes were within 25 points of each other. 43% were party-line: the parties were more than 80 points apart. The rest fell in between.

How a bill comes to the floor matters more than its subject:

  • Fast-tracked bills, which need a two-thirds majority to pass, were bipartisan 87% of the time.
  • Regular bills on final passage were party-line 80% of the time. These are the big, contested bills that make the news.

And these counts understate the agreement. Many bills pass by voice vote, with no recorded roll call, and those are almost always uncontroversial.

Where the parties agree, and where they split

How far apart the two parties voted, by issue. Each bar is the typical gap between the share of Democrats and the share of Republicans voting yes.
  • Among the most divided: energy, environmental protection, immigration, labor, and armed forces and national security. On these, the typical vote had the two parties 84 to 95 points apart.
  • Most bipartisan: science and technology, transportation, emergency management, commerce and international affairs. Here the typical vote had the parties within 10 points of each other.

One caution on taxes. The “Taxation” bar looks fully bipartisan because its seven votes were small, specific bills, such as disaster filing extensions and help for fraud victims. The big 2025 tax-and-spending law (H.R. 1) is classified under “Economics and Public Finance”. Both of its votes were strictly party-line: 0% of Democrats and 99% of Republicans voted yes.

Who crosses party lines?

On the 317 votes where most Democrats and most Republicans voted opposite ways, the typical member sided with the other party about 2% of the time. That’s true in both parties: the median is 2.3% for Democrats and 2.5% for Republicans. Only 41 of the 445 voting members crossed over more than 10% of the time.

Here are the members of each party who crossed most often:

Democrats With the other party Republicans With the other party
Henry Cuellar (TX-28) 48% Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-1) 30%
Don Davis (NC-1) 42% Mike Lawler (NY-17) 14%
Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (WA-3) 40% Thomas Massie (KY-4) 14%
Jared Golden (ME-2) 39% Don Bacon (NE-2) 11%
Vicente Gonzalez (TX-34) 37% Andrew Garbarino (NY-2) 11%

There are two different kinds of crossing in that list:

  • Most cross from the middle. Nearly all of these members belong to the Problem Solvers Caucus or the Blue Dog Coalition, and they vote yes on almost every bill both parties support (98–100%).
  • Massie crosses from the edge. He votes yes on only 56% of the bills both parties back, against 99% for the typical Republican. The members who cross from the middle sit at 98–100%.

My previous post found that this second pattern, voting no on bills both parties back, is the House’s second dimension. It is also what sets the Freedom Caucus apart.

Crossing party lines isn’t good or bad in itself. It can reflect a district, a caucus, a principle or a deal. These numbers describe what happened, not why.

Look up your own representative

How your representative votes is a free, non-partisan dashboard built from the same data. It works the same way for all 445 voting members. Pick your state and representative to see:

  • how often they voted, and how often they sided with the other party;
  • where they sit among every other member;
  • their recent votes on bills, each linked to the bill on Congress.gov, with a filter by issue.

Don’t know who your representative is? Enter your address at house.gov. You can also see every member on a map of the House.

Then vote

Election Day is Tuesday, November 3. Every House seat is on the ballot. You can check your registration, find your polling place and see what’s on your ballot at vote.gov.

The record is public so that voters can use it. Whoever you support, look at what your representative did, then go vote.

Methods

Data.

  • Votes: Voteview (Lewis, Poole, Rosenthal, Boche, Rudkin & Sonnet). The files were downloaded on 2026-10-17 and cover the 119th House’s 674 recorded votes, from January 3, 2025 to September 16, 2026.
  • Topics: the Congress.gov API (Library of Congress). The Congressional Research Service assigns every bill one policy area, plus subject terms and a summary. All 429 bills that received a roll call were found.
  • Senate votes, voice votes and committee votes aren’t included.

Definitions. Everything is computed directly from the votes, with no model.

  • Yes-rate: the share of a party’s members voting on a roll call who voted yes.
  • Gap: the difference between the Democratic and Republican yes-rates (0 = voted alike, 1 = strict party line). Bipartisan means a gap under 0.25; party-line means a gap over 0.8.
  • Votes on bills are final-passage, fast-track (suspension) and amendment votes. Procedural votes, such as the rule that sets up debate, are left out of the issue analysis. An amendment takes its bill’s policy area.
  • With the other party: on votes where the two parties’ majorities voted opposite ways (317 votes, procedural rule votes excluded), the share where a member sided with the other party’s majority.
  • Delegates from DC and the territories are excluded from the comparisons, because they can vote on amendments but not on final passage.

Limits.

  • Each bill gets only one policy area, so a broad bill sits under one heading.
  • The data-center finding rests on a single bill. The bill’s official summary is the only place that names data centers; no subject term does.
  • Caucus labels come from Wikipedia’s current member lists (retrieved 2026-10-17). The Freedom Caucus doesn’t publish its roster.

Code and data: github.com/godot107/ideology-clusters (scripts/fetch_bills.py, scripts/issues.py, app/).

These are public officials’ public votes, described the same way for every member of both parties. This post doesn’t endorse any candidate or party.
entry.summary: A non-partisan look at the U.S. House record before Election Day — which issues bring the parties together, who crosses party lines, and a dashboard to look up your own representative.

entry.title: Finding the factions in Congress from votes alone

link.title: Finding the factions in Congress from votes alone

entry.content:
Every recorded vote in the House is public. How much can you learn about who stands where, and which methods can you trust?

The standard data-science tutorial on this goes: download Congress’s roll-call votes, run PCA or k-means, and watch the Democrats and Republicans fall into two neat clouds. It looks impressive, and it proves almost nothing. Any method separates the two parties. The interesting questions are inside each party: who sits where, how sure can we be, and are there real factions or just a smooth spread?

I compared three ways of placing members on a map and five ways of finding groups, and checked each one against answers the votes never saw. Code, results and executed notebooks: github.com/godot107/ideology-clusters.

The trap: “it separates the parties” proves little

Lay the votes out as a table, one row per member, one column per vote, yes or no in each cell. Plain PCA on the 118th House (2023-24) matches DW-NOMINATE, political science’s standard scores, at a correlation of 0.97. That sounds like a near-perfect result.

Now score it within each party, the way you’d need it to work if you wanted to know which Democrats are more progressive or which Republicans are more hard-line. The agreement drops to 0.52 among Democrats and 0.82 among Republicans. Almost all of that 0.97 came from the two parties being far apart. So every method in this project is scored within party, and splitting the parties counts for nothing.

Grading against a Congress I built

The catch with real votes is that nobody knows members’ “true” positions. DW-NOMINATE is a useful comparison, but it’s a model too: it pools each member’s whole career. So I also built a synthetic Congress: 440 members in six factions, with positions I chose, noisy votes and realistic absences (chronic absentees, members who joined late). There, every method can be graded exactly.

Method Ordering within party (D / R) Full 2-D map recovered
PCA 0.88 / 0.90 0.61
Logistic PCA 0.99 / 0.99 0.95

The difference is how they handle missed votes. PCA treats yes/no as numbers and fills each missing vote with an average, which drags absentees toward the middle. Logistic PCA models the chance of a yes and simply skips votes that weren’t cast.

How many dimensions does Congress have?

On real votes there’s no answer key, so I hid a random 10% of the 118th House’s votes and predicted them. The rival to beat is trivial: “every member votes with their party’s majority”.

Predictor Hidden votes right
Vote with your party 92.8%
Logistic PCA, 1 dimension 95.5%
2 / 3 dimensions 96.1% / 96.3%

The party rule alone gets 93%. One left-right scale adds less than 3 points, and extra dimensions add less than one more. That matches decades of political science: modern Congress is close to one-dimensional.

Error bars, and when they lie

A position without an error bar hides how much the data actually supports it. So I fitted the standard Bayesian ideal-point model (Clinton, Jackman & Rivers, 2004) in NumPyro, which gives every member a range.

Every member of the 118th House, ordered by position, with a 90% range

The wide ranges make sense once you look at who has them: members sworn in late after a special election, members who left early, and members at the far edge of their party, where no vote separates them from their neighbours. Within party, this model agrees best with DW-NOMINATE: 0.90 among Republicans and 0.72 among Democrats (0.89 and 0.75 in the current House).

But the synthetic Congress caught something. For five of the six factions, the 90% ranges contained the true position 77-91% of the time, close to the promised 90%. For the sixth, a faction I’d made different on a second dimension (voting against its own leadership), they contained it only 25% of the time. A one-dimensional model has nowhere to put that difference, so it squeezes those members onto the left-right line and reports narrow ranges around the wrong spot. Error bars are only as honest as the model behind them.

The fix is to give the model somewhere to put it. With a second dimension, the same faction’s ranges contain the truth 93% of the time on left-right (95% on the second dimension), and the other five stay at 82-97%. Getting there took one more lesson: these models only loosely fix where the axes point, so the sampler’s runs slowly drift and rotate, and the raw diagnostics looked like total failure. Lining every draw up on a common map (a rotation that moves nobody relative to anybody else) showed the runs had agreed all along.

Factions: five methods, one trade-off

Next, clustering. I compared k-means with a Gaussian mixture (soft membership: “70% this group”), HDBSCAN (dense regions, with members in between as noise), Ward hierarchical clustering, and community detection on a co-voting network. Each picked its own number of groups by its standard rule.

On the synthetic Congress, the honest finding was this: k-means, the mixture and Ward all found three groups (Democrats, Republicans and the faction that differs in kind). The factions that differed only by degree (a wing, a mainstream, moderates) formed a continuum with no gap between them, so there was nothing to find. Telling k-means the “right” answer of six groups made it score worse, because it then cuts the continuum at arbitrary points.

On the current 119th House, I checked each method against caucus membership, which the votes never saw. F1 measures how well one cluster captures a caucus within its party (1 = exactly). Stability is how similar the clustering stays when the roll calls are resampled (1 = identical).

Method Groups Freedom Caucus Progressive Caucus Blue Dogs Stability
k-means 3 0.55 0.63 0.63 0.95
Gaussian mixture 5 0.59 0.66 0.31 0.75
HDBSCAN 2 0.24 0.62 0.05 0.97
Ward 3 0.70 0.61 0.09 0.87
Network communities 5 0.61 0.82 0.15 0.68
119th House on two dimensions, coloured by Gaussian-mixture group, with Freedom Caucus and Progressive Caucus members marked

Explore the map yourself: hover over any member, highlight a caucus, or search by name.

The methods that find the most faction structure are the least stable. HDBSCAN is rock-steady because it mostly just returns the two parties. Network communities isolate most of the Progressive Caucus but reshuffle the most between resamples. There’s no single best method. The useful habit is to report clusters together with their stability, and to use soft membership for the 86 members who don’t belong more than 80% to any one group.

So what is the second dimension?

In the map, Freedom Caucus members sit at the bottom of the Republican cloud. The axis has no label of its own, so I went back to the votes. For every roll call where at least 5% of a party broke with its majority, I asked which dimension predicts who broke away.

Among Republicans, left-right barely does (correlation 0.07). Dimension 2 does (0.36), and most clearly on “suspension” bills, the fast-tracked, two-thirds-majority bills that are in practice the bipartisan ones (0.61). One reading fits both parties: dimension 2 tracks how often a member votes yes on bills that both parties’ majorities support. Across the 80 such votes in the current House, the rank correlation is 0.88 among Democrats and 0.88 among Republicans.

The median Freedom Caucus member voted yes on 53% of those bipartisan bills. Other Republicans: 99%. The Progressive Caucus sits lower than other Democrats too (88% vs 97%), but nowhere near as far.

One caution: the positions were estimated from these same votes, so this describes the axis rather than proving anything about it. The independent part is the caucus comparison, since the caucus lists never went into the model. This is also exactly the kind of group the synthetic Congress warned about: one that differs on a second dimension, where a one-dimensional model’s error bars miss.

So I fitted the two-dimensional Bayesian model to the current House too, to get error bars on both axes. On dimension 2, 30 of the 31 Freedom Caucus members have a 90% range lying entirely below the median of other Republicans. That isn’t automatic: only a third of the other Republicans do. Their ranges are also narrow (half as wide as other Republicans’), so the gap isn’t a few noisy members.

The second axis also changes the first. Among Republicans, the one-dimensional scale and DW-NOMINATE’s first dimension both largely are the bipartisan-bills pattern (rank correlation with the yes-rate -0.85 and -0.76). Once the model has a separate axis for it, its left-right scale barely relates to that pattern (-0.16), and agrees much less with DW-NOMINATE among Republicans (0.54, down from 0.89). The median Freedom Caucus member moves from the 93rd percentile of Republicans on the one-dimensional scale to the 66th on the two-dimensional left-right axis.

In other words, much of what puts them at the far end of a one-dimensional scale is voting no on bills both parties back. A caveat: a two-dimensional model doesn’t fix which way its axes point. I lined them up with logistic PCA’s map, so this split is one reading of the same positions, not the only one.

Polarisation since 1973

Finally I fitted every Congress from 1973 to 2025 separately and measured the gap between the party medians in “typical party widths”. It’s a scale-free measure, so different years can be compared.

Separation, overlap and party-line voting in the House and Senate, 1973-2025

In the House the gap grew from 1.9 party widths in 1973 to about 7 today. My series tracks DW-NOMINATE’s closely (correlation 0.98 in the House, 0.89 in the Senate), and so does the share of party-line votes taken straight from the raw data with no model at all. Since the early 2000s essentially no member is closer to the other party’s median than to their own.

The two models disagree about the 1970s: about 1 member in 5 overlapped the other party by my one-dimensional fit, but 1 in 20 by DW-NOMINATE. That era’s cross-party votes (notably Southern Democrats) ran partly along a second dimension, and a one-dimensional fit squeezes them onto left-right. It’s the same failure the synthetic Congress showed, appearing in real history.

What I’d tell someone running this analysis

  1. Score within party. The party split is free. Report the 0.52, not the 0.97.
  2. Build an answer key. A simulation with known positions is the only place a method can be graded exactly. DW-NOMINATE is a comparison, not the truth.
  3. Beat the party rule. “Vote with your party” already predicts 93% of votes, so a model has to clear that.
  4. Don’t trust error bars from a model that can’t represent the thing you’re measuring.
  5. Report clusters with their stability. A clustering that changes when you resample isn’t a finding yet.

Methods

For readers who want to check the work or repeat it. Everything is in the repository, and one command re-runs each stage.

Data. Every roll-call vote comes from Voteview (Lewis, Poole, Rosenthal, Boche, Rudkin & Sonnet), the standard public database of congressional votes. For each Congress and chamber, it provides three files: the members (with their DW-NOMINATE scores), every member’s vote on every roll call, and a description of each roll call. The files were downloaded on 2026-10-17, so the 119th House covers votes from January 3, 2025 to September 16, 2026. Caucus membership comes from Wikipedia’s current member lists, retrieved the same day. The Freedom Caucus doesn’t publish its roster, so that list covers publicly identified members. Members were matched to the lists by state and district, then checked by surname so that a seat that changed hands isn’t credited to the wrong person. The caucus lists were used only to grade the results, never as an input.

Pre-processing.

  • Each vote becomes a 1 (any kind of yes), a 0 (any kind of no), or blank (present, not voting, or not yet in office).
  • Voteview also records the President’s announced positions as if he were a member, so I removed them.
  • Following DW-NOMINATE’s conventions, I dropped near-unanimous roll calls, where the losing side had under 2.5% of the votes (naming a post office tells you nothing about ideology). I also dropped members with fewer than 20 remaining votes.
  • That left 451 members and 1,119 roll calls in the 118th House (of 1,235), and 448 members and 573 roll calls in the 119th (of 674). About 7% of the cells are blank.

Placing members.

  • PCA fills each blank with that roll call’s average yes-rate, then finds the directions of greatest variation.
  • Logistic PCA models the probability of a yes as a logistic function of a few member and roll-call coordinates. It fits only the votes that were cast, using L-BFGS with an L2 penalty on the coordinates.
  • Bayesian ideal points are the Clinton–Jackman–Rivers model in NumPyro, sampled with NUTS. The priors are Normal(0, 1) for positions and Normal(0, 5) for each roll call’s cut point and direction.
    • One-dimensional fits: two chains of 1,000 warm-up and 1,000 kept draws for the 119th House, and one chain of 500 + 500 for the 118th.
    • Two-dimensional fits: two chains of 1,000 + 500. The most party-line vote is held to dimension 1 to fix the rotation.
    • Because these models only loosely pin where the axes sit, each draw is standardised (1-D) or rotated onto the logistic-PCA map (2-D) before scoring. After that, R-hat is at most 1.04, with no divergent transitions.
  • In every method, the axes are flipped if needed so that Republicans come out on the positive side.

Choosing settings (hyperparameters). No setting was tuned against DW-NOMINATE or the caucus lists, since those are what the results are graded on.

  • Logistic PCA has two settings: the number of dimensions and the penalty strength. Both were chosen by hiding a random 10% of the 118th House’s votes and predicting them. I tried 1, 2 and 3 dimensions with penalties of 0.3, 1, 3 and 10.
    • A penalty of 1 was within 0.05 points of the best and was used throughout.
    • Two dimensions were used for the maps and clusters. A third added only 0.2 points (96.1% vs 96.3%).
  • Clustering methods each chose their own number of groups by their standard rule, so none was told the answer:
Method Settings How the number of groups was chosen
k-means 10 random starts best silhouette score, k from 2 to 8
Gaussian mixture full covariance, 5 starts lowest BIC, k from 1 to 8
HDBSCAN minimum cluster size 10 found by the algorithm; members between groups are left unassigned
Ward (hierarchical) Ward linkage best silhouette score, k from 2 to 8
Network communities each member linked to the 15 colleagues they agree with most Louvain modularity

The embedding-based methods ran on the standardised two-dimensional logistic-PCA positions. The network method ran on the raw votes. To show what a hand-picked k does, I also ran k-means with k fixed at the synthetic Congress’s true 6. It scored worse than letting the silhouette choose (adjusted Rand index 0.42 vs 0.58).

Checks.

  • Synthetic Congress: 440 members in six factions, 1,000 roll calls, and one Republican faction set apart on a second dimension. Most members miss 3% of votes, a few chronic absentees miss 20-50%, and 12 members arrive late or leave early. Positions are scored by within-party rank correlation, and clusters by the adjusted Rand index against the true factions.
  • Caucus F1: for each caucus, the cluster that best matches its members within their party.
  • Stability: resample the roll calls with replacement 20 times, re-fit and re-cluster each time, and take the median adjusted Rand index against the full-data clustering.
  • Error bars: 90% ranges from the posterior draws, checked for coverage on the synthetic Congress.

Polarisation.

  • For each Congress from the 93rd (1973) to the 119th, I fitted a one-dimensional logistic PCA to each chamber separately.
  • Separation is the gap between the party medians divided by the average within-party standard deviation.
  • Overlap is the share of members closer to the other party’s median than to their own.
  • Party-line share is the share of roll calls where the two parties’ majorities voted opposite ways. It is computed straight from the votes, with no model.

These are public officials’ public votes, described with the methods’ own neutral terms.
entry.summary: PCA, logistic PCA and Bayesian ideal points on US House roll calls, graded against a synthetic Congress, and five clustering methods checked against caucus membership.

entry.title: Your model’s score is an estimate. Here’s how wrong it can be.

link.title: Your model’s score is an estimate. Here’s how wrong it can be.

entry.content:
Eight experiments where the right answer is known, so every evaluation shortcut can be graded.

Every machine-learning model arrives with a number attached: 92% accuracy, an AUC of 0.85, an R² of 0.3. Teams ship on that number, budgets get set by it, and model A beats model B because of it. But the number is an estimate of how the model will do on data it hasn’t seen, and nobody usually checks how good that estimate is, because on real data you can’t: the future isn’t in the dataset.

So I built a lab where you can. Every dataset in it comes from a simulation whose rules I wrote, which means that, besides the usual evaluation, every model can also be scored on 100,000 fresh examples from the same rules. That fresh-data score is the truth. The gap between it and what the evaluation reported is the thing each experiment measures. Code, results and an executed notebook: github.com/godot107/eval-lab.

1. Accuracy can’t tell your model from doing nothing

Take a problem where 1 case in 100 is positive: fraud, a machine failure, a disease. My model scored 99.0% accuracy. So did a “model” that answers “no” to everything.

Lesson 1: metrics as positives get rarer, calibration of a class-weighted model, and cost by threshold.

As positives get rarer (left panel), ROC AUC stays roughly flat (0.84 to 0.87), because it only asks whether positives rank above negatives. The precision-recall score falls from 0.84 to 0.14, because it asks how many flagged cases are real, and with rare events most flags are false alarms. For rare events, look at precision and recall.

The middle panel shows a subtler trap. A common fix for imbalance is to weight the rare class more (class_weight="balanced"). Its ROC AUC is identical to the plain model’s (0.861 vs 0.862), so a ranking metric sees nothing wrong. But it now says “34% chance” for events that happen 10% of the time. Every probability is inflated. Only scores that grade the probabilities themselves (log loss, Brier score) and a calibration plot catch it.

That matters as soon as a decision is made. If missing a positive costs 5 and a false alarm costs 1, the right rule is to act when the probability is above 1/(1+5) = 0.167, not 0.5. On fresh data that rule cost 0.292 per case, within 0.007 of the best possible; the default 0.5 cost 0.398. The same 0.167 rule applied to the “balanced” model cost 0.560, the worst option tested, because its numbers only look like probabilities.

On a real dataset, German credit (1,000 loans, 30% go bad, a bad approval costs five times a wrongly rejected good customer), both models at the default 0.5 threshold cost more per loan than simply rejecting every applicant. At the cost-based threshold the logistic model cost 0.54 per loan, against 0.70 for rejecting everyone. Same model; better decision rule.

2. In regression, the metric picks the winner

On a skewed target like house prices or sales, I trained five models, each aimed at a different metric, and scored all of them on all metrics:

Lesson 2: each metric crowns its own model; interval coverage by noise level.

Each metric crowned the model built for it (left). Absolute error rewards predicting the median. Percentage error (MAPE) rewards predicting below the median: it treats a 10% miss on a $5 item like a 10% miss on a $5,000 one, and pays you to forecast low. Only the squared-error model was unbiased on average; the median-type models, including the common habit of fitting log(price) and converting back, under-predicted by about 11%. Fine for a typical house; a problem if the forecasts are added up into an inventory order or a budget.

One result went against the textbook: the squared-error model should have won on RMSE, and it tied with the median model instead. The best possible mean and median predictions differ by only 3% in RMSE here, and 5,000 rows of a skewed target aren’t enough to estimate the mean that precisely. RMSE is dominated by a few huge values.

Two more traps. R² is not a property of the model: the same model with the same error scored R² 0.57 or 0.92, depending only on how spread out the inputs were in the sample. And an “80% prediction interval” can be 80% on average and wrong everywhere (right panel): the usual “prediction plus or minus 1.28 standard errors” contained 99% of outcomes where things were calm and only 64% where they were volatile, exactly where the interval matters. Conformalized quantile regression came closest to the true interval at every level of noise.

3. Even honest cross-validation is noisy

Cross-validation is the standard answer to “how good is my model?”. I trained the same simple model on 200 independent datasets of 200 rows and compared each cross-validation score with the truth:

Lesson 3: cross-validation estimates against the true error over 200 datasets.

On average, 10-fold CV is almost exactly right. For any one dataset, it is typically 3.6 percentage points off, and a single train/test split is about 1.7 times as noisy. Most surprising is the right panel: whether the CV score was high or low barely related to whether that particular model was good or bad (correlation 0.18). This is a known result (Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, Elements of Statistical Learning, 7.12): cross-validation tells you how good the recipe is on average, not the one cake you baked. A 27% error estimate means “roughly 20% to 34%”.

4. Leakage: three ways to fool yourself

Lesson 4: three kinds of leakage, each against the truth.
  • Choosing features before cross-validating. Fifty examples, 5,000 random features, labels that are coin flips: no model can beat 50% error. Pick the 100 features most related to the label using all the data, then cross-validate, and the error comes out at 1.3%. The selection had already seen the test answers. Done inside each fold, the estimate is 48.7%.
  • The same patient in training and test. With ten records per patient, ordinary cross-validation said AUC 0.73; on genuinely new patients the model scored 0.68. Splitting by patient said 0.66.
  • Overlapping time windows. On a price series with nothing to predict, each target covered the next 20 days, so neighbouring rows were near-copies. Shuffled cross-validation reported a small positive R² (+0.02), a model that seems to have an edge. On fresh data it scored -0.20: it loses. Splitting by time got it right (-0.22).

A detour worth admitting: my first check of when “purging” (removing training rows whose time windows overlap the test period) matters gave absurd numbers, R² of -7. The bug was the metric, not the data. Averaging R² fold by fold fails when test blocks are short, because overlapping targets barely vary inside a block. Scored on all predictions together, the answer is sensible: purging barely matters with 5 folds and matters with many folds and long windows.

5. Tuning makes the winning score optimistic

Try 100 settings and keep the one with the best cross-validation score. That score is the winner of 100 noisy estimates, so it’s lucky by construction:

Lesson 5: the winning score after tuning, against nested cross-validation and the truth.

On pure noise (true error 50%), the best of 100 settings claimed 39.9%. On a problem with real signal, the winner claimed 34.9% and truly scored 43.0%, no better than the winner of 10. Nested cross-validation, which wraps the whole tuning process in an outer loop, reported 48.3% and 43.2%: honest both times.

The same thing happens when the validation set is a single group. In an earlier project I tuned a machine-fault detector on one machine and tested it on another, and a 0.96 validation score became 0.61. Here, choosing on one held-out group claimed 27.5% error against a true 40.2%. Cross-validating across all groups claimed 35.4% against a true 38.0%, and chose better.

6. “B beats A” is usually not established

Two models that are equally good by construction, compared with five common statistical tests on 500 datasets. A test at the 5% level should declare a winner at most 5% of the time:

Lesson 6: how often each test declares a winner, when the models are equal and when B is better.

The t-test on repeated random train/test splits declared a winner 45% of the time. The corrected version (Nadeau and Bengio, 2003), the 5x2 cross-validation test and McNemar’s test all kept their promise (5%); a paired t-test on 10-fold CV was mildly over (8%). The sobering part is the right panel: when B really was 6 points better, the tests that kept their promise detected it only 12% to 23% of the time with 300 rows. On small data, “no significant difference” is the expected outcome even when there is one.

7. Will more data help?

Lesson 7: learning curves for a high-bias and a high-variance model, and a validation curve.

Learning curves answer this before you pay for more data. A nearest-neighbour model (second) memorises the training data (error 0) and keeps improving as data grows: more data helps. And the validation curve (right) shows cross-validation picking the right tree depth, while the training error would have picked the most complex tree.

8. Putting it together

The last lesson is a reusable report for any scikit-learn classifier, in the spirit of the “model quality” report AWS’s AutoML service produces. It sets aside an untouched holdout first, builds a leaderboard with a do-nothing baseline, proper scores, calibration, the expected cost of decisions and uncertainty intervals, then scores the winner once on the holdout. Lesson 8: the model-quality report on German credit.

What I’d tell a team

  1. Start from the decision, not the metric. Write down what a miss and a false alarm cost; let that pick the metric and the threshold. Accuracy and the 0.5 threshold are almost never the right defaults.
  2. Check probabilities, not just rankings. Log loss, Brier score and a calibration plot; recalibrate if needed.
  3. Treat every score as an estimate with an error bar. A few points of noise is normal; differences smaller than that need a proper paired test.
  4. Split the way the model will be used. New patients, new machines, the future: the split should look like that.
  5. Keep one set of data that no decision has touched, and use it once.

entry.title: A/B testing my own dashboard, and the ways it tried to lie to me | Willie Man

link.title: A/B testing my own dashboard, and the ways it tried to lie to me | Willie Man

entry.content:
An end-to-end A/B test on the Hiring Demand Monitor, a dashboard I built on Indeed Hiring Lab’s public Job Postings Index. Work in progress: the method and the pipeline are done, and no real-traffic result exists yet. Source: github.com/godot107/ab-lab.

Running an A/B test is easy. Splitting traffic is a few lines of code. What’s hard is everything around it: making sure the two groups really are comparable, deciding in advance what “better” means, and not fooling yourself when the numbers come in.

So I built the whole thing on a dashboard I’d already made, end to end: assignment, logging, a written pre-registration, the analysis, and a stakeholder brief. This post is mostly about the places where it would have produced a confident, wrong answer if I hadn’t caught them first.

Why a hiring dashboard

I started with a question about the job market, not about A/B testing.

The US unemployment rate is low by historical standards: 4.2% in the September 2026 jobs report. On that number alone, it’s a good time to be looking for work. It doesn’t always feel that way, though, and part of the reason is that unemployment and hiring measure different things. The unemployment rate counts people who are looking for a job. Job postings count employers who are looking for people. The two can move apart for a long time.

Indeed Hiring Lab, Indeed’s economic research team, publishes the second one openly: a daily Job Postings Index for the US and other countries, broken out by occupational sector, set to 100 on February 1, 2020, and released on GitHub under CC BY 4.0. It’s one of the best free views of labor demand there is, and nearly every number below comes from it.

The post-pandemic shape is striking once you plot it:

  • The drop. US postings fell to about 62 by early May 2020, nearly 40% below the pre-pandemic baseline.
  • The boom. They passed the baseline within a year and peaked at 161 on March 31, 2022, when employers were advertising roughly 60% more openings than before the pandemic.
  • The long cool-down. From there they eased back for more than four years: 143 at the start of 2023, 120 at the start of 2024, 111 at the start of 2025, and touching 100, the pre-pandemic level, in June 2026. As of September 25, 2026, the index stands at 103.8.

The national number hides a split by sector. Healthcare is far above its 2020 baseline: physicians & surgeons at about 199, therapy at 186. Much of tech and knowledge work sits well below it: software development at 78, IT infrastructure at 69, and data & analytics, the field I work in, at 62. Some of those are recovering (software development is up from 64 a year ago). They are still below where they were before the pandemic.

So “the job market” is really several job markets. I wanted a tool that answers one question for a weekly review: where is employer hiring demand growing, and how broad is it? That became the Hiring Demand Monitor, a Plotly Dash dashboard with a data-quality suite that checks the data before anything renders. Each sector’s move is compared against its own normal variation, so a +0.7% wobble doesn’t get the same bold color as a +37% jump.

Once it existed, I had a real product with a real design question about how its page should be laid out. That is what the rest of this post is about.

The question

The Hiring Demand Monitor opens with a headline, a row of four KPI tiles, then a national trend chart and a ranking of 47 occupational sectors. Almost every mark can be clicked to open a drill-through: the rows behind the number, with the arithmetic shown.

The test asks one thing: does putting the charts above the tiles get more people to drill into the data? Tiles answer “what’s the number?” and can end the visit. A chart answers it while raising “why?”, and here “why?” is one click away. It could just as easily go the other way: charts are slower to read, and someone who wanted a number might leave.

The decision metric is the share of visitors who open at least one drill-through. One metric, chosen before any data arrived.

How it works, briefly

  • Assignment is a hash, not a coin flip. hash(visitor_id + salt) % 100 < 50 → A, else B. The same visitor gets the same version forever, with no lookup table, and the analysis can recompute every assignment to audit the server.
  • The server writes an explicit exposure row at the moment it assigns a version. Splitting traffic at the proxy would have been tidier, but without that row a broken randomizer is undiagnosable.
  • One exposure per visitor is enforced by a database index, not application code. A double-counted visitor silently corrupts the denominator of every rate.
  • The browser never says which version it’s in. Every event’s version is recomputed on the server from the cookie.
  • The live stats endpoint returns counts, never a p-value. More on why below.

All of it is a small package ( ablab) that mounts on the dashboard's Flask server, so the dashboard itself only asks "which version is this visitor in?"

Where it tried to lie to me

1. My first treatment was a guaranteed null

My first idea was a colour test. The ranking colors a sector’s bar only when its move is beyond a ±3σ “normal variation” limit, and grey otherwise. Version B would colour every bar.

I wired it up, opened both versions side by side, and they looked almost identical. At the default “compare to 1 year” setting, nearly every sector’s move is beyond its limit, so the two versions differed by one grey bar out of twenty.

That test would have run for a month and come back “no significant difference”. The tempting reading is “colour doesn’t matter”. The real reason would have been that I never changed anything. I swapped it for the layout test before writing the pre-registration.

Lesson: look at the arms before you measure them.

2. The dashboard would have changed itself mid-test

Both versions have to show the same content for the whole test, so the daily data refresh is switched off while an experiment runs. Simple enough.

But the dashboard also runs a data-quality suite, including a blocking freshness check: data more than 14 days old turns the header badge red and tells every visitor to treat the numbers as unverified. The original deploy restarted the app daily, re-running the checks. So about two weeks into a 28-day test, the page would have changed under both versions at once, in a way that plausibly affects whether anyone trusts the numbers enough to click into them.

The fix: while an experiment is live, the freshness check reports “frozen for experiment X” instead of failing. It still shows the age; it just doesn’t sound the alarm.

3. On a phone, A and B look the same

I took screenshots of both versions on desktop and mobile for reference, and the mobile pair was a surprise.

The treatment is much weaker on phones. That isn’t fixable inside this test without changing the design, so it’s written into the pre-registration as a known threat, and any per-device result is labelled exploratory.

4. A true effect that came back “inconclusive”

The real experiment needs traffic a personal site won’t get: at 250 visitors per version, the smallest effect it can reliably detect is about 12 percentage points. So the method is checked separately with synthetic visitors whose true effect I set by hand, sent through the real site over real HTTP.

With a true lift of +12 points for B, one run measured +12.05 points, 95% CI [+4.6, +19.5]: the pipeline recovers what it was given.

Another run, same settings, measured +5.6 points with p = 0.14: inconclusive. Nothing was broken; the generator’s own random draws just came up low. A third came in at +18.6. At this sample size the test has about 80% power, so roughly one run in five misses a real +12-point effect, and the ones that catch it can overshoot it by half.

That’s the most important thing the project says, so the readout says it explicitly: not significant means not measurable below this size, not “no effect”.

5. Peeking turns 5% into 28%

The obvious way to run a test is to check it every day and stop when it looks significant. The simulation measures what that does to the false-positive rate when there is no real effect at all:

Checking daily for a month and stopping at the first p < 0.05 makes a false win about five times as likely. Hence the fixed stopping rule (250 visitors per version or 28 days, analyzed once), an endpoint that never shows a p-value, and a stakeholder brief that refuses to compare A and B until the rule is met. Mid-test, it only reports progress, data health and pooled usage.

The live status page follows the same rule. Here it is partway through a demo run, with 202 visitors, 200 of them synthetic and labelled as such:

The same simulation caught a bug in my own sample-size formula: a missing factor of 2 that had every power calculation understating the traffic needed by half.

6. The smaller ones

  • A test that started failing on a date. The dashboard’s smoke test checked data freshness against the real clock, and its synthetic data ended on a fixed date. It passed for two weeks after that date, then failed every day after. It now pins “today”.
  • Two claims I had to take back. My own code comment said a drill-through was “a click the browser can’t fabricate”. It can, for its own cookie; what it can’t do is choose its version. And an inherited line said first-time visitors were reported separately. They weren’t. Both are corrected rather than quietly left in.
  • The first cloud deploy failed with “command not found”. The EC2 instance registered with AWS Systems Manager while its own setup script was still running, before it had written the deploy script it was about to be asked to run. A one-line wait fixed it.

What “better” means here

Written down before any data, in this order:

  1. Check the split. Visitors should divide about 50/50. If they don’t (p < 0.001), the pipeline is broken and nothing is read.
  2. One decision metric: drill-through rate. B wins only if it’s higher and the 95% interval for the difference stays above zero. Anything else is inconclusive, and A stays.
  3. Supporting numbers that never decide: time on page (median seconds the tab was visible), quick exits, repeat drill-throughs, which chart people clicked first.

What isn’t measured yet: page-load time and JavaScript errors. Until they are, a “win” can’t rule out a version that’s slower or broken, and the readout says so.

Where it stands

The method, the pipeline and the deploy are done and tested, including a live demo on AWS. The real 28-day run hasn’t happened. If it does, it will most likely come back inconclusive, and the write-up will say exactly that, with the size of effect it could have detected.

The full pre-registration, the sample stakeholder briefs and the code are in the repository.

Data and credit

All job-postings data comes from Indeed Hiring Lab’s Job Postings Index ( hiringlab.org · data.indeed.com · github.com/hiring-lab/job_postings_tracker), licensed CC BY 4.0. Source: Indeed Hiring Lab. Thanks to the Hiring Lab team for publishing it openly. The unemployment figure is from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Employment Situation release for September 2026. This is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Indeed.
